publisher_issuer: Wikipedia (corroborating named journalism: Reuters, FT, CNN, CNBC)
company_context: Wirecard AG was a Munich-headquartered DAX-listed payment processing and financial services company. In June 2020 its long-time auditor EY refused to sign off on the 2019 accounts after being unable to verify EUR 1.9 billion of cash supposedly held in escrow accounts in Asia. The company admitted the cash likely did not exist and filed for insolvency on 25 June 2020.
evidence_summary: Auditor EY could not confirm EUR 1.9 billion of cash purportedly held in trustee accounts in the Philippines/Asia; Wirecard conceded the funds likely did not exist. The fraud combined fabricated third-party acquiring (TPA) revenue with money laundering over many years. CEO Markus Braun resigned and was arrested on suspicion of inflating the balance sheet and revenue through fake transactions; COO Jan Marsalek fled. German regulator BaFin had taken little action and had targeted short-sellers and critics rather than the company. Wirecard filed for insolvency on 25 June 2020, the first DAX member to do so.

source_backed_metrics.fraud_duration_years_approx: over two decades of fraudulent practices alleged

outcome_evidence: Wirecard filed for insolvency on 25 June 2020 after admitting EUR 1.9 billion was missing and likely never existed; CEO Markus Braun was arrested; it became one of the largest financial scandals in post-war German history.
source_limitations: Primary regulator pages (BaFin) and SEC-equivalent releases not fetched; figures here are drawn from Wikipedia summary corroborated verbatim by Reuters/FT/CNN/CNBC search snippets. Wikipedia is a tertiary source; rating reflects strong multi-outlet corroboration rather than a single primary filing fetched.

why_useful_for_opsiq: Archetypal accounting/governance fraud where reported financials were fabricated; the 'obvious' move (trust audited cash balances and reported revenue) is exactly the trap. Tests OpsIQ's ability to flag legal_governance_risk and route to governed re-evaluation when reported evidence is itself suspect, and to distinguish reported health from real solvency.
